content: The global estimates for 2012 indicated that there were approximately 217,678 live births affected by congenital syphilis among 1,360,485 pregnant women with untreated syphilis. This translates to about 16 live births with congenital syphilis per 100 untreated women. These figures do not include stillbirths (21 per 100), neonatal deaths (9 per 100), or premature births (6 per 100). Hospitalization costs for infants with congenital syphilis are more than three times higher than for infants without the disease. This highlights the significant resource implications of untreated syphilis during pregnancy. A systematic review conducted by Shahrook in 2014 identified two cluster randomized controlled trials, but no new trials were found when the search was updated to September 2016. These trials did not compare different rapid syphilis tests (RST) directly to each other. Moderate-quality evidence suggests that congenital syphilis is likely reduced with RST screening (45 fewer cases per 1,000; range: 50–14 fewer). Screening coverage is likely higher with RST (100% with RST vs. 80% with RPR + TPHA), and treatment rates are also likely higher (99% vs. 90%). Partner treatment rates are similarly higher with RST (95% vs. 55%). A study by Myer in 2003 compared on-site RPR testing to laboratory-based RPR testing but only followed women who tested positive. Low-quality evidence suggests that perinatal deaths may be reduced with on-site rapid testing (18 fewer per 1,000; range: 36 fewer to 22 more). Treatment rates may be slightly higher with on-site RPR (69% vs. 64%), but screening coverage may be similar. A systematic review of 10 studies assessed the sensitivity and specificity of various syphilis tests, including Visitect® Syphilis, SD Bioline Syphilis, and on-site RPR, compared to laboratory-based gold standard tests (RPR or VDRL followed by TPPA or TPHA if positive). The certainty of evidence was rated as moderate due to concerns about bias, selective reporting, and heterogeneity. Not all studies could be included in the meta-analysis, and the largest study, which carried the most weight, did not apply the reference standard to all positive cases. Results for the single on-site RPR test strategy were inconsistent across studies and dependent on the setting. The consequences of treatment, over-treatment, and missed treatment were adapted from the 2016 WHO guidelines for syphilis treatment. The evidence suggests that using a single on-site RST followed by treatment (Strategy A) or an on-site RST followed by a confirmatory RPR test and further treatment if positive (Strategy C) may result in slightly to moderately higher treatment rates compared to on-site RPR strategies (Strategies B and C). In low-prevalence settings, the difference in over-treatment between RST and RPR strategies is trivial, but in high-prevalence settings, the difference may be moderate, favoring the RST strategy. The number of pregnant women screened appears to be slightly higher with the single on-site RST strategy (Strategy A) but similar across other strategies and prevalence settings. The GDG agreed that more value should be placed on missed cases of syphilis due to the serious adverse effects of syphilis in pregnancy, including congenital syphilis and fetal death. Cost-effectiveness analyses indicate that the single on-site RST strategy (Strategy A) is the most cost-effective approach across all prevalence settings, although it may cost more in certain settings. Mass treatment was found to be the most cost-effective in high-prevalence settings but resulted in more over-treatment. The GDG agreed that cost-effectiveness favored on-site RST strategies. There is no direct evidence measuring the impact of test strategies on health equity. However, the GDG noted that while the cost of RST may be higher for pregnant women in some countries, screening rates achieved with RST appear to be slightly higher, suggesting that such costs may not reduce equity. If screening coverage is greater with RST, equity may be increased. Additional research on the effect of higher costs to pregnant women on equity and accessibility is warranted. Acceptability of RST was demonstrated in several studies. Pregnant women preferred RST over RPR due to same-day testing and treatment, which saved time and travel costs. Health workers found RST easier to perform and more reliable than RPR. Integration of RST into existing services was well-received, and its introduction led to policy changes in some countries to incorporate RST into national guidelines. Feasibility of implementation depends on high-quality training for healthcare providers on testing procedures, counseling, and quality assurance systems. Regular supervision and support are also necessary to ensure successful implementation.
